## Summary

Documentation-only refresh that brings the README table of contents back in sync with the headings actually present in the file, and updates `docs/architecture.md` so its diagram and descriptions match the current code.

The README had drifted: three sections (`Features`, `Verification`, and `Use as an SSH ProxyCommand`) exist in the body but were missing from the table of contents. The architecture doc was likewise stale in three places — its component diagram predated `lib/cli_main.rb`, the Dockerfile description understated which executables land on `PATH`, and the `ssm-jump` target-resolution algorithm omitted the input validation step that rejects malformed targets.

- Add the missing `Features`, `Verification`, and `Use as an SSH ProxyCommand` entries to the README table of contents, nested at the correct depth
- Extend the architecture diagram to show `lib/cli_main.rb` (`CliMain`) as a shared dependency of the top-level scripts alongside the AWS SDK, covering shared errors and option parsing
- Document the `ssm-jump` `--autoselect-first` flag, which takes the first matching instance instead of prompting
- Correct the Dockerfile description to state that seven executables are symlinked into `/usr/local/bin` without their `.rb` suffix, and note that `sync-jira-release` is shipped in the image but not placed on `PATH`
- Update the target-resolution algorithm to include the `^[a-z0-9\-]+$` guard on `tag:Name` lookups and the fatal error for targets that match none of the accepted forms

items.title: docs(readme): sync README with ADRs 033-046
items.body:
## Why

`README.md` had not been touched since 2026-05-25. Fourteen ADRs landed after it (033–046), several of which invalidated statements on the front page — most visibly, the README still described **two** local engines with **Whisper** as the default and cloud providers as *"planned"*, when five engines ship today and **Parakeet is the default**.

This is a docs-only change. No source files were touched.

## What changed

**Engines** ([ADR-033](docs/decisions/033-translation-model-capability.md), [041](docs/decisions/041-parakeet-v3-sherpa-onnx.md), [042](docs/decisions/042-parakeet-default-language-ux.md), [043](docs/decisions/043-cloud-speech-providers-v1.md))
- Added an engine comparison table (5 engines: where each runs, download size, languages, translation).
- New Parakeet section — CPU-only, ~670 MB INT8 default plus the fp32 entry, 25 European languages always auto-detected, RTF ≈ 0.07–0.13.
- New Cloud providers section — OpenAI-compatible + xAI Grok, BYOK, base-URL rules, dialog-based error surfacing.
- *Provider Modes* rewritten from "planned" to shipped, including the persistent Cloud badge.
- Whisper's translate-to-English toggle documented as model-gated.

**Languages & translation** ([ADR-034](docs/decisions/034-source-target-language-selection.md), [036](docs/decisions/036-language-ux-rebuild.md), [037](docs/decisions/037-gemma4-source-target-prompts.md), [042](docs/decisions/042-parakeet-default-language-ux.md))
- New section: the `[source] → [target]` relationship row, keyboard-layout source sentinel, per-engine target forms (toggle / full / disabled), fallback-with-toast on engine switch, and the Language page hiding entirely for auto-detect-only engines.
- Gemma 4 prompt tokens are now `{speech_lang}` / `{text_lang}` (`{language}` retired).

**Transcribe widget** ([ADR-038](docs/decisions/038-speech-model-prewarm-and-loading-state.md), [040](docs/decisions/040-frameless-compact-transcribe-window.md), [042](docs/decisions/042-parakeet-default-language-ux.md))
- New section: frameless 172×88 card (118 px with the language strip), grip-strip drag, Esc hides, position persistence with off-screen self-heal, deferred load spinner, opt-in preload toggle.

**Privacy & Security** ([ADR-046](docs/decisions/046-security-hardening-batch.md))
- New section: transcripts never logged, clipboard-history exclusion, SHA-256 download verification, DPAPI key storage, HTTPS-only cloud base URLs, atomic settings writes.
- New table of what Parlotype stores under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\parlotype\` (`settings.json`, `window-state.json`, `secrets.json`, `models\`, `logs\`).

**Build & structure** ([ADR-044](docs/decisions/044-microbenchmark-project.md), [045](docs/decisions/045-audio-pipeline-allocation-threading.md))
- `Parlotype.MicroBenchmarks` added to the project tree, with its run command and the deliberate quality-vs-allocation distinction.
- Architecture section now describes the three-stage channel pipeline and the pooled (zero-allocation) capture path.
- Added a Parakeet smoke-test benchmark example and the `-p:EnableCuda=false` build variant.

**Stale facts corrected**
- `Settings → Runtime` → `Settings → Speech engine → Whisper runtime`.
- GPU acceleration scoped to Whisper (it previously read as app-wide; Parakeet is CPU-only by design).
- Tech stack gained sherpa-onnx, ZLogger, DPAPI, BenchmarkDotNet.
- Whisper model size range corrected to 75 MiB – 2.9 GiB (was "75 MB – 1.6 GB", which omitted Large v1/v2/v3).

## Reviewer notes

Two judgment calls worth a look:

1. **Release zip sizes** — I replaced the specific `Lite ~720 MB, Full ~870 MB` with "roughly 0.8–1 GB unzipped; exact sizes are listed on each release." Those figures predate the sherpa-onnx native libraries and I could not measure the published artifacts. If you have current numbers, they're better than my range.
2. **Gemma 4 languages** — the old README said "English-only for now", but `SpeechEngineCapabilities.For(Gemma4)` grants the full catalog plus arbitrary translation. I documented the capability and kept the quality caveat ("best on clean English speech", marked Experimental), matching the engine card copy in `SpeechEngineSettingsViewModel`.

- All `docs/decisions/*` and `docs/security/*` links in the README were checked to resolve against files on disk.
- Facts were sourced from the ADRs and then confirmed against current code (`SpeechEngine`, `SpeechEngineCapabilities`, `WhisperModelInfo`, `ParakeetModelInfo`, `Gemma4ModelInfo`, `SettingsKeys`, section `Title` overrides, `TranscribeWindow.axaml(.cs)`, `Parlotype.slnx`, Platform path constants) rather than taken from the ADRs alone.
- No build or test run: docs-only, no compiled files touched.

## Out of scope

Definition-of-Done item 4 (memory vault) is **not** addressed — `memory/services/*.md` and `memory/architecture/subsystems.md` may carry the same staleness the README had. This PR was deliberately scoped to the README; the vault audit is a good follow-up.

items.title: docs: sync README, deploy, MCP, and env docs with recent changes
items.body:
The docs had drifted from the code across the last several merges. Everything here was checked against the source rather than restated from the commit history.

## What was actually wrong

**Counts that no longer matched the code**
- Skills counted 8; there are 9. `mqtt-top-talkers` shipped with the TimescaleDB work and never made the list. The MCP server registers one prompt per `skills/*/SKILL.md`, so `docs/mcp-server.md`'s "8 skill prompts" was wrong for the same root cause. Both fixed, with a note that the prompt count is derived so it stays self-correcting.
- K8s tools said 15; `tools/k8s.py` defines 16. All of them are now named rather than trailing off in a `...`.

**Tooling that was registered but undocumented**
- `timescale_query` appeared in no doc at all — not the README, not `.env.example`. Added the tool with its read-only safety model (dedicated read-only role, read-only transaction, single `SELECT`/`WITH` only, statement timeout + row cap) and the fact that it is not registered unless `TIMESCALE_PASSWORD` is set.
- The git (5) and github (9) tool families are registered in `tools/__init__.py` but were absent from the README tree.

**Deployment reality**
- `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` listed 2 workloads; there are 7. MCP and bridge reuse the agent image and roll with it; worker, executor, and changerecord have their own images built by separate jobs of the *same* workflow, tracking the floating `:main` tag and deliberately outside the auto-bump — so the "merge the bump PR" path does not apply to them.
- Recorded what the image contains and why `auth/` and `scripts/` have to be in it: `web_server.py` and `mcp_server/server.py` both import `auth.bootstrap` at module load, so a missing `COPY` crash-loops the pod rather than degrading it. That is the failure this repo hit, and `test_dockerfile_image.py` now guards it.
- "Common Change Types" now covers `auth/`, `scripts/`, `mcp_server/`, `bridge/`, and the sibling images.

**CI was undocumented**
- No doc mentioned `tests.yml`. It is the only automated gate between a branch and an image — the build workflow does not run tests. The suite also cannot run as one flat `pytest` (colliding top-level module names, bare imports needing their own directory on `sys.path`), so the per-directory `PYTHONPATH` invocations are written down in both the README and the copilot instructions.

**Factual errors in `.github/copilot-instructions.md`**
- `web_server.py` described as a FastAPI app; it is Flask served by Waitress, which is also why the WebSocket path is disabled.
- Skills described as "YAML-defined runbooks"; they are `SKILL.md` (YAML frontmatter + markdown playbook).
- Missing every directory added since the file was written: `auth/`, `mcp_server/`, `bridge/`, `executor/`, `changerecord/`, `worker/`, `scripts/`.

**Config**
- `.env.example` had no `TIMESCALE_*` block and no console auth section, despite `CFOP_SESSION_SECRET` being required for sessions to survive a restart.

**Navigation**
- The README documentation index covered 6 of 18 docs. It now covers all of them, grouped by what the reader is trying to do.

## Notes

- `docs/auth.md` was left alone — #105/#108 kept it current.
- Two links in `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` point at the sibling `homelab-infra` repo and do not resolve in this checkout. Pre-existing; not touched. Every other relative link in the changed files was verified to resolve.
- **This merge does build a new image.** An earlier draft of this description claimed otherwise. `.env.example` is not matched by any of the build workflow's `paths-ignore` patterns (`**.md`, `docs/**`, `benchmarks/**`, `cfassist*/**`, `cfshared/**`, `llm-gateway/**`, `grafana/**`, `observability/**`), so pushing this to `main` triggers `build-cfoperator-main.yml` and opens an auto-bump PR on homelab-infra. The image content is unchanged — `.env.example` is not COPYed into it — but the deploy machinery does fire.
- No executable file changed: the diff is 4 `.md` files plus `.env.example`. Nothing in the test suite reads `.env.example` (the `.env` references in `conftest.py` and `test_event_runtime.py` are to the gitignored real `.env`), so this PR cannot move a test outcome.

Neuroscience & Cognitive Science benchmarks for LLM/VLM agents: a three-way read-only sweep → deep-checked in four batches → 5 cards (en + zh), wired, and audited. Scope ruling applied strictly: only benchmarks evaluating LLMs/VLMs/agents on neuroscience/psychology **research** tasks.

### New cards (10 files, en + zh) — all under Scientific Agent Benchmarks + the Neuroscience & Cognitive Science domain

- **BrainBench (EEG)** (2608.04156) — instruction-conditioned EEG analysis across 4 subsets / 17 datasets / 100K+ executions (distinct from the documented BrainBench)
- **Rodent-Bench** (2602.18540) — multimodal-LLM annotation of real rodent behavior video across neuroscience paradigms
- **CPsyExam** (2405.10212, COLING 2025) — Chinese psychology examination benchmark (22k pool → 4k)
- **PsychCounsel-Bench** (2510.01611) — ~2,252 U.S. counselor-certification questions
- **ConceptPsy** (2311.09861) — concept-level psychology benchmark (12 subjects, 1,383 concepts)

- Neuroscience & Cognitive Science domain 5 → 10; Scientific Agent Benchmarks topic 135 → 140; card total 217 → 222; both READMEs and the topics/README taxonomy count synced
- Exact en/zh row + Related Works parity (141/141 topic, 11/11 domain), two-way topic sync, 13 headings per card, no broken links

### Scope notes (why only 5)

This field yielded few reusable LLM-research benchmarks; most candidates were disqualified:
- **Out of scope:** CheeseBench (the LLM is a behavioral *subject* scored vs animal cognition — a cognitive-capability probe), ConnectomeBench2 (pure computer-vision, no language model)
- **Parked frameworks/systems:** SeekBrain/BrainArena, NeuroAgent, Automated Cognitive Scientist, GeCCo, Neurodata Without Boredom, the fly-optogenetics case study, KG-Driven Neuroscience Reasoning
- **Separate domains/clusters:** the clinical/psychiatric assessment cluster (MentalBench, PsychBench, PSYCHE, MAGI…) belongs to Medicine & Health (its own sweep); the cognitive-capability cluster (theory-of-mind, WorM, CogBench, personality/MOSAIC…) parked per the ruling

BrainBench (EEG) is carded distinct from the documented BrainBench with an explicit collision note (there are now four distinct "BrainBench" works in the literature). items.title: Add scriptc static-compilation example with benchmark
items.body: ## What An end-to-end example (\`examples/scriptc/\`) testing whether inrepo-vendored dependency source lets [scriptc](https://github.com/vercel-labs/scriptc) compile dependencies **statically**, instead of falling back to \`--dynamic\` mode (which embeds QuickJS and bundles the package JS), and benchmarking the difference. A small terminal app (commander + picocolors) is built two ways from identical app logic: | variant | deps from | scriptc mode | binary | avg run (mitata, spawn/iter) | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | \`demo-vendored\` | \`inrepo_modules/\` | **static** | 750 KB | **2.05 ms** | | \`demo-npm\` | \`node_modules/\` | \`--dynamic\` | 1.2 MB | 15.66 ms | | baseline | — | \`bun cli.ts\` | — | 22.72 ms | | baseline | — | \`node cli.ts\` | — | 62.39 ms | Both binaries produce byte-identical output and exit codes across greet/help/version/error/suggestion paths. Apple M5 Pro, scriptc 0.0.25. ## Why this is an inrepo showcase scriptc can only statically compile source it can see and type-check — npm artifacts don't qualify, but a pinned, patched vendored checkout does. The committed overlays in \`inrepo_patches/\` are what make upstream compile: JSDoc type tightening (scriptc enforces JSDoc at runtime — this surfaced two genuine upstream commander type bugs, one of which segfaulted the binary), union narrowing around commander's getter/setter methods, and restatements for stdlib gaps (EventEmitter → Map-based emitter, \`fn.apply\`, \`Promise.then\`, \`Object.assign\`, g-flag \`match()\`, sparse array writes). Effective delta: ~715 added / 240 removed lines against ~4,000 upstream lines in touched files; commander's \`argument.js\`/\`error.js\`/\`index.js\` needed nothing. \`inrepo sync\` reproduces the compiled tree exactly (including tracked file deletions via \`.inrepo-deletions\`) and \`inrepo verify\` passes. ## Layout - \`cli.ts\` / \`cli-vendored.ts\` — the two variants (differ only in imports + a zero-arg action callback) - \`inrepo.json\` / \`inrepo.lock.json\` — pins - \`inrepo_patches/\` — committed overlays (generated \`inrepo_modules/\` is gitignored; rebuild with \`npx inrepo sync\`) - \`bench.ts\` — mitata spawn benchmark - \`README.md\` — full writeup incl. reproduction steps ## Follow-ups The experiment surfaced inrepo feature gaps (patch-maintenance UX), filed as #49 (inrepo diff), #50 (upgrade/re-merge workflow), #51 (transitive dep vendoring), and #52 (patch provenance). --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. Autofix is disabled.

items.body:
## Why

The table gave four rows of percentages with no way for a reader to tell which are strong, which are bounded, and which are the honest weak spots. Adds a `#` column and a numbered walkthrough beneath it — one entry per row, each stating what was measured **and what the number does not establish**.

## Three things the table stated but did not explain

**Row 1 — "harmless-twin refusal 100.0%" reads like an achievement.** It is the friction extreme: the benign twin of every task was blocked too, all of them. CLAIM-002's own caveat is explicit — *"FAR=0.0% is the hard safety floor; FBR documents friction"* — so the walkthrough now says plainly that this measures a system refusing the whole category rather than one that separates harmful from harmless.

**Row 2 — the headline "700 tasks" is 70 templates × 10 cosmetic variants.** The `effective N = 70` caveat was already in Scope; the walkthrough adds the two things CLAIM-001 explicitly instructs readers not to get wrong: the baseline gap is *not* statistically separable (p=0.50), and the floor comes from the deterministic hard blocks, not the ensemble.

**Row 3 — the weakest number is the informative one.** 10.9% of known-wrong calls were accepted (28/258, against a ≤20% bar). A call can be structurally perfect and still aim at the wrong target; that is the current limit of the routing layer.

Row 4 is framed as what it is: a regression guard over 167 previously observed failures — evidence that old bugs stay fixed, and nothing more.

## Budget

README stays at **exactly the 200-line hard cap**. The added ~20 lines were paid for by tightening the "Try it" link lists, the intro blurb and the closing paragraph, and by rendering the walkthrough as a list (list items need no blank separators).

items.title: Add CodSpeed performance benchmarks and CI integration
items.body:
## Summary

This PR sets up continuous performance measurement with CodSpeed for the deterministic calculation engines in `scripts/`.

The project is a pure-standard-library Python codebase with three hot-path modules that are called on every ticker analysis. This adds a benchmark harness that measures them and tracks performance on every push and pull request.

## Changes

- **Benchmark harness (`pytest-codspeed`)**: Added `pytest-codspeed` as a dev dependency via `uv`, initializing `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock` (the project previously had no package manager). `scripts/` is placed on the pytest `pythonpath` so the modules import cleanly.
- **Benchmarks (`benchmarks/`)**: 8 benchmarks covering the performance-critical paths, run against realistic ~290-bar synthetic close-price series:
  - `test_indicators.py` — full indicator stack (`compute`) plus individual primitives (`ema_series`, `rsi_wilder`, `macd`, `trix`).
  - `test_macro_pillar.py` — cross-asset macro-sentiment scorer (`score_macro`) with a full 8-ETF payload.
  - `test_score.py` — three-pillar scoring/decision engine (`score_symbol`) for both holding and flat scenarios.
  - `_data.py` — shared deterministic data generators mirroring the modules' self-test series.
- **CI workflow (`.github/workflows/codspeed.yml`)**: Runs benchmarks on pushes to `main`, pull requests, and manual dispatch. Uses OIDC authentication, `CodSpeedHQ/action@v4` in `simulation` mode on `ubuntu-latest`, with dependencies installed via `uv sync`.
- **README badge**: Added the CodSpeed badge.

## Local verification

All 8 benchmarks pass locally in simulation mode and upload to CodSpeed:

```
test_compute_full_stack     4.08 ms
test_ema_series            87.68 µs
test_macd                 840.66 µs
test_rsi_wilder             1.10 ms
test_trix                   1.11 ms
test_score_macro            1.57 ms
test_score_symbol_flat      4.13 ms
test_score_symbol_holding   3.76 ms
```

## Next steps

- Merge to establish the performance baseline on `main`.
- Future PRs will automatically report performance deltas against that baseline.
- Consider adding benchmarks for additional input sizes or edge cases as the calculation logic evolves.

items.title: Add ProgramBench benchmark runner
items.body:
## Summary
Adds an end-to-end **ProgramBench** runner, config, docs, and tests. ProgramBench gives an agent only a program's *compiled binary + documentation* and asks it to reconstruct a source tree (with a `./compile.sh`) that reproduces the program's behavior. Each instance runs in its own real per-instance **Docker sandbox** (via `opensandbox`) under the official anti-cheat network isolation, and submissions are scored with the official `programbench eval`.

## What's added
| File | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `examples/run_programbench.py` | MetaAgent runner over selected instances (`--task-ids` / `--start/--end`), `--evolve/--no-evolve` toggle, per-instance Docker sandbox, submission extraction. |
| `configs/programbench_agent.py` | Base roster for code reconstruction (meta/code/general/reviewer + `bash_tool`); evolution roster imported & configured but appended only at runtime under `--evolve`. |
| `examples/README_programbench.md` | How to set up, run, and score the benchmark, plus gotchas. |
| `tests/test_run_programbench.py` | Unit tests for selection/roster/prompt helpers. |
| `pyproject.toml` | Adds `programbench` (benchmark extra) and `opensandbox`/`opensandbox-server` (sandbox extra). |
| `agentevolver/sandbox/*`, `agentevolver/agent/types.py` | Sandbox wiring + fixes (see below). |

## Key design
- **Per-instance Docker sandbox**: `sandbox_manager.acquire("opensandbox", image="<image_name>:task_cleanroom_v6", …)`; `opensandbox-server` auto-starts on `localhost:28080`.
- **Network isolation ON by default** (`--network none`, the baseline's anti-cheat); toggle with `AGENTEVOLVER_SANDBOX_ISOLATE_NETWORK=0`.
- **`bash_tool` only**: file/git tools are excluded (not sandbox-aware); all file/git work routes through the container via `bash_tool`.
- Runs tasks only; scoring is the separate official `programbench eval` (rebuild via `compile.sh` + hidden test suite).

## Notable fixes along the way
- **Workspace path**: surface the in-container `/workspace` in the agent prompt when a container sandbox is bound (new `Sandbox.container_workspace`). Previously the prompt reported the *host* workspace path, so agents wrote deliverables to a path the container never saw and `extract_submission()` (which tars `/workspace`) lost them.
- `execution_to_result()` no longer crashes on non-zero-exit sandbox commands.
- `SandboxConfig.network` wired through to opensandbox `NetworkPolicy`.
- `SandboxServerManager` domain wired to the server's own bind port.
- Roster trimmed to sandbox-aware components only.

## How to run / score
\`\`\`bash
pip install -e ".[benchmark,sandbox]"     # + a working Docker daemon
python examples/run_programbench.py \
  --task-ids abishekvashok__cmatrix.5c082c6,wfxr__csview.8ac4de0 \
  --cfg-options model_name=google/gemini-3.1-pro-preview
# scoring: see examples/README_programbench.md (programbench blob sync + programbench eval)
\`\`\`

## Testing
- `pytest tests/test_run_programbench.py`
- Verified end-to-end on 2 instances with the official evaluator (default params): both compile and run against the hidden test suites and produce non-zero scores. (Agent-quality scores are high-variance run-to-run; the runner/scoring path itself is deterministic.)

## Notes
- Task images (`…:task_cleanroom_v6`, ~4 GB) are pulled on first use; pre-pull to avoid the sandbox-create timeout.
- Test blobs come from `programbench/ProgramBench-Tests` on HuggingFace (per-instance sync supported; no full 12 GB download needed for a few tasks).

items.title: test(sync): pin a reach stated as a fraction of the fleet (#958)
items.body:
Closes #958.

## What was unguarded

`AGENTS.md` L178-179 says it "is distributed to six of the eleven members while that one reaches all eleven". Both numbers come straight out of `studio.config.json`, and nothing checked either.

The existing sweep in `member-count.test.mjs` pins two shapes: a bare fleet size, and the `all N members` form added in #842/#880. A fraction is neither. `six of the eleven members` asserts the fleet is eleven just as flatly as `eleven members` does, and it additionally asserts a reach — the part most likely to go stale, because opt-in flags move in the manifest and no prose moves with them.

## Checked against the engine, not against the manifest

The #842 reach rule treats a qualified count as a *bound* — it may be anything up to the fleet size. That is all you can do without knowing which document the sentence is about.

Here the subject is recoverable, so the number is checked exactly. `sync/test/canon-audience.mjs` resolves every member through `resolveAll` + `enumerateTargets` and builds a document to audience map over all 62 written sources. A numerator is then compared with the members that actually receive that document.

| document | audience |
| --- | --- |
| `copilot-instructions.md` | 11 |
| `instructions/workflow.instructions.md` | 9 |
| `instructions/tokens.instructions.md` | 7 |
| `AGENTS.md` | 6 |
| `instructions/infrastructure-operations.instructions.md` | 2 |
| `docs/sync.md` | 0 (no canon kind covers `docs/`) |

Four claims are live. All four are true today: `AGENTS.md` 6/11 about itself, `docs/sync.md` 0/11 about itself, and `docs/sync.md` + `sync/README.md` both at 9/11 about `instructions/workflow.instructions.md`.

Attribution is nearest preceding mention inside 300 characters, with `this file` / `this document` resolving to the containing document. **A claim that names no document fails.** It cannot be checked, which makes it the shape that decays quietly, so it is treated as a fault rather than skipped.

That rule caught a sentence I had just written in `sync/README.md` describing this very guard. It named no subject, so it was unverifiable — fixed by naming `docs/sync.md`, which genuinely holds the claim. A live positive off the tree, not a fixture.

## Keeping true prose writable

Thirty-odd fractions in the tree are historical narrative or genuine subsets: "three of six", "Twelve of the thirteen repositories", "one of nine members holds a". A guard that fires on correct past-tense prose gets weakened or deleted, which is already stated twice in this file.

The **definite article** separates them. `the eleven members` names the whole population; `eleven members` names some eleven. That discriminator yields exactly the four claims above and touches none of the narrative.

Zero words (`no`, `none`, `zero`) are included so `docs/sync.md`'s `none of the eleven members` is seen — a numeral-only pattern misses it. They are added in a local `FRACTION_WORDS` map rather than to the shared `WORD_NUMBERS`, which feeds `ANY_COUNT_PHRASE`; that pattern has no `all` requirement and would have widened silently.

## Controls

Eight mutants, each killed by a distinct named failing test:

```
A  FLEET_FRACTION requires "all" again (the #246 blind spot)   KILLED  1
B  zero-words dropped from the fraction map                    KILLED  1
C  reachFault never faults on the numerator                    KILLED  2
D  reachFault stops checking the denominator                   KILLED  1
E  subjectOf never attributes                                  KILLED  2
F  subjectOf drops the self-reference branch                   KILLED  2
G  audienceOf stops treating "not canon" as zero               KILLED  2
H  the audience map narrowed to one kind                       KILLED  3
```

Plus two standing controls: one that the phrasings swept for are the ones that appear, and one that the predicate fires on a deliberately wrong input, so a population of zero cannot be mistaken for a pass.

## Two instrument errors, recorded in the code

Both are written into the `canon-audience.mjs` header, because the reasoning is the reason the file is slow on purpose.

**A merged-plan enumeration silently dropped all 21 skills documents.** Dir kinds name their specs `<group>/<file>` rather than after the group, so the key derivation missed an entire class. All four document-named controls passed anyway — none of them was a skill — and so did a `>= 40` size floor, at 41. **That floor had been written by reading the already-broken output**, so it was pinned to the defect and could never have falsified it.

**The benchmark that justified it had measured a warm cache.** The shortcut "measured" 36s to 1.3s, but it ran second, after the eleven-member walk had already warmed git's object cache. Cold, in fresh processes, in both orders: 25s vs 36s. Eleven seconds does not buy subtle key derivation plus an oracle, so the optimization was **withdrawn** and the plain memoized enumeration kept. An inflated benchmark buys a design decision as well as a wrong number, and the design outlives the correction.

Both lessons are added to `instructions/workflow.instructions.md`.

## Gates

```
node --test "sync/test/*.test.mjs"        432/432   (was 427)
node --test "principles/test/*.test.mjs"   16/16
node sync/index.mjs --dry-run             exit 0
```

All three re-run after rebasing onto the current `main`.

items.title: fix(ci): #4211 — sync the conformance docs AFTER the high-water raise, not before
items.body:
The recurring `quality` failure that has blocked every open PR three times today, traced to its cause rather than patched again.

## Symptom

```
[sync-conformance] DIFFERS  README.md (standalone)
  committed: **standalone (host-free) test262 conformance**: 28,257 / 43,505 (65.0 %)
  generated: **standalone (host-free) test262 conformance**: 28,270 / 43,505 (65.0 %)
```

The mismatch is between **main's own README** and **main's own committed artifacts** — nothing to do with the PR being tested. It clears only when some unrelated PR happens to carry a `sync:conformance` commit, and returns on the next baseline bump.

Seen three times on 2026-08-07 (28,222→28,227, then 28,257→28,270), and it parked **nine PRs** that morning. #4178 repaired that instance without finding the cause.

## Root cause

`sync-conformance-numbers.mjs` derives **two** numbers from **two different files**:

| line | source |
|---|---|
| JS-host conformance | `benchmarks/results/test262-current.json` |
| **standalone (host-free)** | **`benchmarks/results/test262-standalone-highwater.json`** |

In `baseline-summary-sync.yml` the order was:

1. copy the fresh `test262-current.json`
2. **run `sync-conformance-numbers.mjs`** ← reads the *old* high-water mark
3. **`check-standalone-highwater.mjs --update`** ← raises the mark
4. `git add` the mark **and** the README, and commit

So one commit carries a **new mark** and a README synced from the **old** one. Not a race, not flaky — a deterministic inconsistency emitted **every time the mark rises**.

The `promote-baseline` job in `test262-sharded.yml` carries a comment insisting this sync "must update everything derived from it ATOMICALLY in the same commit". That intent was right; this job silently broke it, because the standalone half derives from an artifact written *later in the same job*.

The **re-anchor / retry path** had the same defect in subtler form: it re-applies the snapshotted README — already synced against the *original* mark — then recomputes the mark against main's freshly fetched tip (`max(ours, main's)`), and never re-syncs.

## Fix

- **Fresh path** — the sync now runs *after* the raise, when both inputs are final.
- **Re-anchor path** — re-run the sync after the recompute, and re-stage `README.md ROADMAP.md CLAUDE.md plan/goals/goal-graph.md`.

`refresh-baseline.yml` already had the correct order (raise ~447, sync ~780) and is **unchanged**. `test262-sharded.yml`'s promote job syncs from an artifact that is already final and is **unchanged**.

## Why chase it instead of patching again

The per-PR repair is one line and takes a minute, which is exactly why it kept being the chosen response. The minute is not the cost:

- it blocks **every** open PR at once, so it scales with queue depth;
- the failure names the **PR's own** `quality` job, so each lane diagnoses it from scratch as though it were their own regression — three lanes did that today;
- it recurs on every baseline bump, several times a day.

## Verification

`baseline-summary-sync.yml` parses (`yaml.safe_load`), and both `sync` calls now follow their corresponding raise — verified by line order: raise 224 → sync 237, raise 333 → sync 343.

**The real proof is behavioural and arrives on the next high-water rise:** main should stay self-consistent and no PR should need a hand-carried sync commit. If one does, this fix is incomplete and there is a third writer — stated in the issue file so the next person isn't misled by a green CI run here.

## Summary

Scope ruling applied: LLM/VLM-agent benchmarks only — pure ML surrogate/property/potential/generation leaderboards rejected at tiering.

### New cards (28 files, en + zh) — all under Scientific Agent Benchmarks + the Materials Science domain

- **Knowledge & reasoning:** MaScQA (650 GATE questions; Digital Discovery), MatSciBench (1,340 college problems; KDD 2026; DeepSeek-R1 75.22% / GPT-5 53.02%), LLM4Mat-Bench (property prediction; NeurIPS 2024 AI4Mat), MatText (crystal-as-text; the "GNN-LM wall")
- **Crystallography:** AtomWorld (structure manipulation; rotations <12%), OpenXRD (217 XRD questions, 74 models; Digital Discovery/RSC)
- **Characterization VLM:** MatVQA (1,325 Q, real microscopy/diffraction), MatCha (1,500 Q, 21 tasks; EMNLP 2025 Findings), MatQnA (10 methods; frontier MLLMs ~90% objective)
- **Extraction / tool-use:** MatViX (324 articles → 1,688 JSON, curve-fidelity metrics), MatTools (pymatgen; 69,225 QA + 49 execution tasks)
